multifamily.heading: Multifamily Financing in Los Angeles: Underwriting Rent Control From Day One
paragraphs: LA multifamily underwriting starts with a question that does not come up in most other metros: is this building subject to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance? Pre-October 1978 buildings fall under RSO, which caps annual rent increases at 4 to 6 percent and layers on just-cause eviction protections, and that ceiling directly shapes the achievable rent growth a lender will underwrite. Post-1978 construction is exempt and underwrites against full market rent, which is why two physically similar apartment buildings a block apart can support very different loan proceeds purely based on their construction date. Sponsors who bring an RSO-aware rent roll analysis to the table, rather than a generic market-rent pro forma, get faster and more accurate quotes.

Value-add multifamily plays are where this matters most: renovating occupied RSO units to push rents requires navigating the city's relocation assistance ordinance, which runs $8,600 to $22,600 per unit depending on tenant tenure before a unit can be taken offline for substantial rehab. That cost has to be underwritten into the business plan alongside the renovation budget itself, and Measure ULA adds a further layer at exit: a sale above $5.3 million inside City of LA boundaries carries a 4 percent transfer tax, 5.5 percent above $10.6 million, which sponsors need to model against their projected disposition value from the start rather than discover at closing.

Submarket matters as much as building vintage. Koreatown, Westlake, and Mid-Wilshire carry deep value-add multifamily lender appetite despite heavy RSO exposure, because experienced capital sources already understand the relocation math and price accordingly. Newer construction and ED1 or TOC density-bonus projects, which can add 60 to 80 percent more units near transit, draw a different lender set focused on construction and lease-up risk rather than rent-control-constrained cash flow. We place both profiles regularly and structure the loan around which risk actually applies to the specific asset, not a one-size-fits-all LA multifamily template.

Loan size also changes which capital sources actually compete for an LA multifamily deal. Around $5 million sits the sweet spot for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac Small Balance Loan programs, where streamlined agency underwriting produces the fastest execution available for 5 to 50 unit product. From roughly $10 million to $25 million, standard Fannie Mae DUS and Freddie Mac Optigo conventional executions take over as the most competitive source for stabilized market-rate buildings, with life insurance companies competing hardest on Class A and Class B assets in exchange for tighter leverage. Above $35 to $50 million, the deal moves into institutional territory: club bids among life insurance companies, large-loan agency programs, CMBS conduits, and in some cases pension fund or insurance-consortium participations all compete for the same asset, and the negotiating dynamic shifts from picking a lender to running a structured process across several capital sources at once.

industrial.heading: Industrial Financing in Los Angeles: Infill Scarcity Versus New Supply
paragraphs: LA industrial financing splits along a line that matters more here than in most metros: infill product inside the urban core versus newer big-box supply on the periphery. Land-constrained submarkets like Vernon, Commerce, and the central LA industrial corridor have essentially no ability to add new supply, so lenders underwrite existing infill buildings against structurally low vacancy and strong rent growth even when the physical asset is decades old. That scarcity premium is a real underwriting input, not just a talking point, and it is a big part of why infill industrial in LA proper carries different leverage assumptions than comparable-vintage product in a market with open land.

The South Bay, anchored by the ports of LA and Long Beach, and the Inland Empire Gateway submarkets carry the newer, larger-footprint distribution and logistics product that institutional lenders and life companies favor for its modern clear heights, trailer parking, and credit-tenant leases. Manufacturing, cold storage, and flex R&D space scattered through the Valley and central LA tend to draw more bank and bridge capital, since single-tenant owner-user deals and smaller conversions do not fit the box that life company and CMBS underwriting wants.

AB 2011 is increasingly relevant to LA industrial owners specifically because it allows ministerial approval to convert underused commercial and some industrial-zoned parcels to residential without a discretionary entitlement process, which has made older, functionally obsolete industrial buildings a target for repositioning rather than continued industrial use. Sponsors evaluating that path need financing structured around the conversion timeline rather than a standard industrial refinance, and we work both sides: straight industrial holds and industrial-to-residential adaptive reuse plays, depending on which one the specific parcel and zoning actually support.

mixed-use.heading: Mixed-Use Financing in Los Angeles: TOC and AB 2011 Are Reshaping the Asset Class
paragraphs: Mixed-use underwriting in LA has to reconcile two different income streams that often behave differently: the ground-floor commercial space and the residential units above it. When the residential component is RSO-covered, that portion of the rent roll is capped the same way a pure multifamily building would be, while the commercial space underwrites on its own lease terms and tenant credit. Lenders comfortable with LA mixed-use know to underwrite each layer separately rather than blending them into a single average rent assumption, which is exactly the kind of local nuance that trips up out-of-market capital sources.

Transit Oriented Communities density bonuses, which allow 60 to 80 percent more residential units near qualifying transit stops, have made ground-floor-commercial-plus-apartments the default new-construction mixed-use product in corridors along the Metro rail and rapid bus network. AB 2011's ministerial approval path for converting underused commercial corridors to mixed-use residential is accelerating this further, letting sponsors skip the discretionary entitlement process that used to make these deals slow and uncertain to underwrite for construction lenders. Both mechanisms shift LA mixed-use from a niche, hard-to-finance asset class toward one with a defined, increasingly familiar development playbook.

Live-work and adaptive reuse conversions, particularly older commercial buildings repositioned under AB 2011 or Executive Directive 1 where the affordable component qualifies, are the deals where CLS CRE adds the most value: sourcing construction and bridge-to-perm capital from lenders who understand the specific ministerial approval track being used, rather than defaulting to a generic discretionary-entitlement risk premium on a project that may not actually carry that risk.

self-storage.heading: Self-Storage Financing in Los Angeles: Land Cost Drives the Structure More Than Operations
paragraphs: Self-storage economics are famously stable almost everywhere, low turnover, hundreds of independent tenants per facility, minimal capex, but in Los Angeles the binding constraint is land cost and zoning, not operations. Ground-up self-storage development competes for the same infill parcels as multifamily and industrial, and land prices in most LA submarkets no longer pencil for a single-story drive-up facility; nearly all new LA self-storage development is multi-story, climate-controlled, and often built with structured parking or mixed-use ground-floor retail to justify the land basis. Lenders underwriting LA self-storage construction expect that vertical, higher-cost building type as the norm, not the exception.

Conversion plays, industrial or retail buildings repositioned into self-storage, are common in LA precisely because they sidestep the land-cost problem: the sponsor is buying an existing structure and shell rather than raw land, which changes the basis and the loan-to-cost math substantially versus ground-up construction. AB 2011's ministerial approval track does not apply to storage conversions the way it does to residential, so these projects still go through standard commercial permitting at LADBS, and lenders factor that timeline into a conversion's construction-to-stabilization schedule differently than a residential AB 2011 project.

Once stabilized, LA self-storage refinances competitively with banks, life companies, and specialty storage lenders all active in the space, since the asset class's low operating complexity and diversified tenant base underwrite well regardless of submarket. The sponsors who get the best terms are the ones who accurately price the land or conversion-shell cost into their initial construction or acquisition loan rather than assuming stabilized-asset economics apply from day one.
